title: Technical deep dive: Autoscaling & capacity planning

Customer to provide a redacted sample prompt set and representative input length distribution by 2025-11-10
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to review benchmark results and recommended reserved GPU sizing (target week of 2025-11-17)

summary: Deep technical discussion focused on autoscaling strategies (burst policies, queueing), capacity planning for reserved GPUs, and performance knobs (KV cache, batching, quantization). Customer is running a clinical-notes summarization pipeline with spiky traffic; primary concerns: tail latency, cost predictability, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run benchmarks and share sizing recommendations.
transcript: 00:00 Samir (Redwood AE): All right, thanks everyone for joining. Quick intros? 00:12 Rachel (Nimbus VP Eng): Hi it's Rachel, we own platform at Nimbus Health, thanks for doing this deep dive. 00:18 Ethan (SRE): Ethan here, looking after infra and SRE. 00:22 Priya (ML): Priya, ML engineer, I run the summarization model pipelines. 00:26 Samir: Great. Leah from Redwood is our SE, she'll lead on the runtime questions. Leah? 00:30 Leah (Redwood SE): Hi everyone, thanks. I sketched an agenda: current workload profile, autoscaling goals, burst and reserved options, KV cache + batching, and then sizing. Please stop me anytime. 00:45 Rachel: Sounds good. Quick context: we process clinician-entered notes, a mix of short and long sequences. Baseline traffic is low but we get big spikes during morning shift and after chart closures. Our p95 latency target is <600ms for the summarization endpoint, cost is also a big factor, and we must keep PHI inside our VPC. 01:08 Leah: Understood. Is the inference currently hosted on AWS? 01:11 Ethan: Yes, EKS, customers using GPU nodes in a mixed nodepool; right now it's our own stack with Triton for some models and internal batching. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated / Private for predictable performance and better autoscaling. 01:26 Samir: Two quick clarifications — when you say spikes, what's the spike magnitude compared to baseline? 01:31 Rachel: Baseline ~20 reqs/min, spikes up to 600 reqs/min for 10-20 minutes. 01:38 Priya: Sequence lengths vary 32-2k tokens, but 70% are under 256 tokens. 01:44 Leah: That distribution helps. If most are short we can optimize for lower latency but we still need capacity for those long tails. 01:51 Samir: Let's walk through autoscaling patterns: Reactive autoscale based on GPU utilization, queue-based autoscale, and reserved capacity with burst policies. 02:00 Leah: For reactive GPU utilization scaling you typically set GPU util thresholds — e.g., scale up when p95 GPU utilization >75% for 60s — but that can be slow for sudden spikes because of provisioning time. 02:12 Ethan: Right, in our infra node provisioning is ~3-5 minutes which is too long for the spikes. 02:18 Leah: Exactly. So Redwood Dedicated suggests reserved GPU pools sized to handle baseline + a buffer, and then a burst capacity layer. Burst options: pre-warmed ephemeral pods on the same tenant, or cross-tenant burst to lower-cost spare capacity (policy controlled). 02:32 Rachel: Cross-tenant burst worries us because of PHI — we'd only allow same-tenant or private burst within our VPC. 02:39 Leah: That's fine — Private and Dedicated both support VPC-only burst policies. We can do pre-warmed replicas inside your VPC or a small standby pool of reserved GPUs that are cold-start free. 02:50 Priya: Can you explain queueing-based autoscale? We heard about queue regulators that throttle requests to keep p95 latency stable. 02:56 Leah: Sure. Two flavors: client-side rate limiting and server-side queuing. Server-side queuing will accept requests and schedule them to workers; you control max queue length to bound latency. For example, if you allow a queue depth of 50 and each worker averages 100ms per token compute, the queueing delay can blow up — so we prefer short queues with autoscale triggers on queue growth plus token-in-flight metrics. 03:20 Ethan: So queue-size becomes a signal for scaling. What's the tradeoff vs rejecting requests? 03:24 Samir: If you reject requests you avoid latency tail but risk user errors; queuing smooths bursts but adds tail latency. For our customers we often combine short, capped queues with burst capacity to keep p95 under SLO while absorbing spikes. 03:40 Leah: Another lever: KV cache. With a good prefix hit-rate we can avoid recomputing large KV attention states for repeated prompts. For your pipeline, if many requests share similar prefixes (templates), enabling prefix caching reduces avg token compute significantly. 03:55 Priya: We have templated prompts for discharge summaries — likely high cache hit. How do you size cache memory? 03:59 Leah: We estimate KV cache memory based on model size and typical sequence length; e.g., for a 70B model with fp16, each token KV is X bytes — we provided a sizing spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.ai/internal/kv-sizing) and we'll include a simplified version in the benchmark bundle. 04:15 Rachel: Okay. Batching — we currently do custom batching on our side. What's Redwood's approach? 04:20 Leah: Redwood runtime does continuous batching with latency SLO constraints; we form micro-batches frequently and have an adjustable max batch size and max wait time. For short sequences, batching yields huge throughput wins with small latency penalty; for long sequences it can hurt latency. 04:36 Priya: Any quantization tradeoffs? We're worried about quality drop for clinical text. 04:40 Leah: Quantization (int8 / awq / q4f16) gives 2-4x throughput depending on model. Quality regression is model- and task-dependent. We recommend running a quality regression test on your eval set. For clinical text, many customers keep fp16 for the critical path and selectively quantize lower-use variants. We'll run evals in the benchmark. 05:00 Ethan: On the dedicated pool sizing: if we reserve N A100s, how does Redwood map that to pods/instances and how does GPU packing work? 05:10 Leah: We pack multiple worker processes per GPU where appropriate; runtime supports tensor-slicing and model sharding. Reserved capacity maps to a GPU pool that the scheduler allocates from; you can set min and max config and a reserved commit to guarantee throughput. We'll produce a few sizing options: conservative (handle 95th percentile spike), economic (baseline + small buffer + fast burst), and hybrid. 05:33 Samir: Let's do an example. With your spike numbers (600 reqs/min), average request ~0.8s on our 13B fp16 baseline — roughly 1.2 RPS. Actually convert: 600 reqs/min = 10 RPS. With model throughput of about 20 RPS per A100 for short sequences with batching, you'd need ~1 A100 to handle 10 RPS comfortably, but long-tail sequences reduce effective throughput. 06:00 Priya: That math helps but we need specifics on p95. 06:03 Leah: We'll run a synthetic mix: 70% short (<=256 tokens), 30% long. We'll benchmark and show p50/p95/p99 latencies and token cost per request. 06:14 Rachel: On VPC/on-prem — we must ensure KMS integration and no cross-tenant memory sharing. 06:20 Samir: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and customer-managed VPC peering; audit logs are forwarded to your SIEM. We'll attach the security packet (SOC2, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS notes). 06:31 Ethan: For burst policies that use pre-warmed replicas, what's cold-start time? 06:34 Leah: Pre-warmed replicas are essentially warm worker processes with model loaded — cold-start is <5s for most modern backends if model artifact is already present on disk and runtime warmed. If model is not local, image pull + weight load could be 60-120s. That's why we recommend keeping a small number of pre-warm workers for predictable spikes. 06:56 Priya: What about cost estimates of pre-warmed standby GPUs? 06:59 Samir: We can model cost in the spreadsheet: reserved cost + incremental cost of warm but idle workers. Often customers prefer a small standby (1-2 GPUs) to avoid SLA breaches — cheaper than repeated overprovisioning. 07:14 Leah: A quick note on queueing model math: if arrival is Poisson with lambda spikes, and service time distribution heavy-tailed, p99 latency is dominated by long sequences; we mitigate by segregating long sequences to a slow-path pool (different model variant or QoS class) to avoid head-of-line blocking. 07:34 Rachel: Could we route long docs to a background job and return quick summary then refine? 07:38 Priya: That's actually something we already do for nightly batch, but real-time needs are the problem. 07:42 Leah: Routing by policy (latency vs cost) is a Redwood feature — you can send short prompts to fast low-latency variant and long ones to a high-throughput, lower-cost quantized variant. 07:53 Ethan: Any recommendations for autoscaling thresholds? 07:57 Leah: Start with multi-signal autoscaling: queue length, token-in-flight, and GPU util. Example: scale up if queue > 20 for 30s OR token-in-flight > X OR p95 GPU util > 75% for 60s; scale down conservatively with cooldown of 5-10 minutes. 08:16 Samir: We'll include sample HPA/cluster-autoscaler rules and a recommended burst policy config in the follow-up. 08:23 Rachel: What about observability — we need token-level cost and per-route SLOs. 08:27 Leah: Redwood Console exposes token and per-route cost, trace hooks, and model-level dashboards. We'll add the console screenshots and a short walkthrough recording link in the follow-up. 08:40 Priya: For benchmarking, do you need ground truth or do you run with synthetic prompts? 08:43 Leah: Prefer your redacted real prompts for quality regression; synthetic mixed-length workloads are fine for perf. Please include typical top-10 prompt templates. 08:53 Samir: Recapping next steps: Redwood runs benchmarks (Leah), customer sends traffic distribution and prompt set (Ethan/Priya), Samir sends pricing + security docs (Samir). 09:04 Rachel: Good. Also can you include example burst policy configs and a sample reserved GPU sizing worksheet? 09:09 Leah: Yes link to workbook will be included. 09:12 Ethan: One more: can you show how to enforce that burst only uses same-tenant capacity in Private? 09:15 Leah: We'll include the exact policy flag names and an example manifest for VPC-only burst in the follow-up. 09:23 Priya: Thanks — this covers the questions I had. 09:25 Samir: Great — we'll follow up with the benchmark bundle, security packet, and a proposed sizing doc. 09:31 Rachel: Thanks everyone. 09:33 (call ends)
